text: Briarcliff Networks is a fictional managed-services company we'll use to design around a deadline instead of a threshold -- a different kind of problem than Lesson 11's quote approval.

Briarcliff promises a four-hour response on Urgent cases, but there was no internal warning system. Cases quietly blew past the deadline, and the first person to find out was whoever answered the angry phone call.

The design has two moments with two different audiences. An hour before the deadline, the case owner gets a warning. At the deadline, if the case is still open, the owner's manager gets notified, the case is flagged as escalated, and the customer gets an acknowledgment email.
Configured, it's two scheduled actions off the same case record -- a warning at the three-hour mark, and a breach notice at four hours, each reaching a different person with a different message.

The warning fires early enough that the owner still has time to act before anyone above them is looped in. And the breach step only fires if the case is still open -- close it in time, and the scheduled action simply never fires.

Leadership now sees warnings before breaches instead of after a complaint call. Next up: once automation like this is built, how do you document it so the next person doesn't have to reverse-engineer it?
